title: Reading the Letters
summary: The ancient letter and how the New Testament letters use and change it, secretaries and couriers, rhetoric and the diatribe, the art and risk of reading someone else's mail, the household codes and how Christians read them today, and the debates over who wrote which letter.

sections.body:
Twenty-one of the twenty-seven books of the New Testament are letters, or are shaped like letters. Thirteen bear Paul's name. The others are Hebrews, James, 1 and 2 Peter, 1, 2, and 3 John, and Jude, and Revelation opens with seven short letters to churches. The letters are also the oldest Christian writings that survive. Paul's first letter to the Thessalonians, written about AD 50, is probably the earliest book of the New Testament, written some twenty years after the crucifixion and before any of the Gospels.

Letters were how the apostles stayed present to churches they could not visit. Paul's letters often speak of his wish to come in person, and the American scholar Robert Funk, in a 1967 essay, called this recurring feature the apostolic presence (parousia): the letter stood in for the apostle, carrying his authority and his affection until he could arrive. The letters were written to be read aloud to the gathered church. Paul says, “I charge you before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers.” (1 Thessalonians 5:27), and he asks the Colossians to exchange letters with the church at Laodicea (Colossians 4:16).

Copies were made and collected early. 2 Peter already speaks of Paul's letters as a group, noting that “Some parts of his letters are hard to understand” and that people twist them “as they do the rest of the Scriptures” (2 Peter 3:16). The oldest surviving collection of Paul's letters, the papyrus codex known as P46, copied about AD 200, contains most of them, with Hebrews placed right after Romans. In modern Bibles Paul's letters are arranged roughly by length, longest first, with the letters to churches (Romans to 2 Thessalonians) before the letters to individuals (1 Timothy to Philemon). That order has nothing to do with when they were written, and reading them in a likely chronological order is one of the best ways to see Paul's life and thought unfold.

sections.body:
In 1896 and 1897 two Oxford scholars, Bernard Grenfell and Arthur Hunt, began excavating the rubbish mounds of Oxyrhynchus, a town in Egypt, and recovered tens of thousands of papyrus documents, among them a vast number of ordinary letters: a son asking his mother for money, a soldier writing home, business instructions, invitations. The German scholar Adolf Deissmann, in Light from the Ancient East (German 1908), used such letters to show that the Greek of the New Testament was the everyday Greek of the Roman world, not a special holy language, and that Paul's letters were real letters addressed to real situations. Deissmann distinguished true letters, private and occasional, from literary epistles written for publication; later scholars have seen that Paul's letters sit between the two, personal and occasional but also public, carefully argued, and intended for more than one hearing.

An ordinary Greek letter had a fixed pattern. It opened with the sender's name, the recipient's name, and a greeting, typically a single word, chairein, ‘greetings’. Two New Testament letters use exactly this form: the letter of the Jerusalem council in Acts 15:23 and the Letter of James (James 1:1), both of which end their opening with “Greetings.” Then often came a wish for the recipient's health or a thanksgiving to the gods, then the body of the letter, and finally closing greetings and a farewell.

Paul keeps the pattern and fills it with the gospel. He expands the sender's name into a description of his calling: “Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle, and set apart for the gospel of God” (Romans 1:1). In place of chairein he writes charis, ‘grace’, a word that sounds like it, and adds eirēnē, ‘peace’, the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew greeting shalom: “Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.” (Romans 1:7). In place of a conventional thanksgiving, he thanks God for what God has done in the church, and his thanksgivings often preview the letter's main themes. The absence of a thanksgiving can be as loud as its presence: Galatians is the only letter of Paul to a church with neither a thanksgiving nor a blessing of God at its opening, and it moves straight from greeting to rebuke, “I am amazed how quickly you are deserting the One who called you” (Galatians 1:6). The body of the letter usually moves from teaching to exhortation (often called paraenesis) and closes with travel plans, requests, greetings to and from named individuals, a final blessing, and sometimes a note in Paul's own hand.

Paul's letters are also unusually long. Most surviving private letters on papyrus run under a hundred words. The letters of Cicero average a few hundred words, and Seneca's literary letters about a thousand. Romans runs to more than seven thousand words. Only a few of the New Testament letters, 2 and 3 John and Philemon, are the length of an ordinary private letter, the amount that would fit on a single sheet of papyrus.

Ancient letters of any length were usually written by a secretary, called an amanuensis, who might take dictation word by word, write from notes, or compose a letter from the author's general instructions, with the author reviewing and approving the result. Paul used secretaries. One of them identifies himself: “I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord.” (Romans 16:22). Several letters end with Paul taking the pen himself to add a greeting or a guarantee: “See what large letters I am using to write to you with my own hand!” (Galatians 6:11); “This greeting is in my own hand—Paul. This is my mark in every letter” (2 Thessalonians 3:17); and in Philemon, a promise to repay any debt the slave Onesimus owes, signed like an IOU, “I, Paul, write this with my own hand. I will repay it” (Philemon 19). The personal signature guaranteed the letter, which mattered because letters falsely claiming to be from Paul were already circulating (2 Thessalonians 2:2).

Most of Paul's letters also name co-senders: Sosthenes in 1 Corinthians, Timothy in 2 Corinthians, Philippians, Colossians, and Philemon, and Silvanus and Timothy in both letters to the Thessalonians. Scholars debate how much these co-senders contributed. 1 Peter says it was written “Through Silvanus” (1 Peter 5:12), which may mean Silvanus was the secretary, the courier, or both. E. Randolph Richards, in The Secretary in the Letters of Paul (1991), surveyed the ancient evidence and argued that because secretaries could be given considerable freedom, differences of vocabulary and style between letters are a weak basis on their own for judging authorship. This bears on the debates over the disputed letters, described below.

There was no public postal service for private individuals in the Roman Empire, so letters were carried by travelers, friends, or trusted messengers. The letter carrier often read the letter aloud and explained it. Phoebe, whom Paul commends to the church in Rome as “a servant of the church in Cenchrea” (Romans 16:1), is widely thought to have carried the letter to the Romans. Tychicus carried Colossians and probably Ephesians (Colossians 4:7-9; Ephesians 6:21-22), and Epaphroditus Philippians (Philippians 2:25-30).

Because letters were read aloud to a gathered church, they were shaped to persuade listeners, and educated writers in the Greco-Roman world learned persuasion through the study of rhetoric. Aristotle had distinguished three kinds of speech: judicial (or forensic), which accuses or defends concerning the past; deliberative, which urges a course of action for the future; and epideictic, which praises or blames in the present. Since the 1970s many scholars have analyzed Paul's letters with these categories. Hans Dieter Betz's commentary on Galatians (Hermeneia, 1979) read the letter as an apologetic speech in the judicial style. George Kennedy (New Testament Interpretation through Rhetorical Criticism, 1984) applied classical rhetoric across the New Testament, and Margaret Mitchell (Paul and the Rhetoric of Reconciliation, 1991) read 1 Corinthians as a deliberative argument for unity. Ben Witherington's many socio-rhetorical commentaries carried the method to a wide readership. Other scholars, such as Stanley Porter and Jeffrey Weima, have cautioned that letters are not speeches and that the handbooks of rhetoric were written for oratory, so that letter-writing conventions are a better guide. The debate is ongoing; its lasting gain is the reminder that Paul argues, and that his letters have a shape and a strategy that repay attention.

One rhetorical style needs special attention because misreading it changes the meaning. The diatribe was a teaching style used by philosophers in their schools, preserved especially in the Discourses of the Stoic teacher Epictetus (recorded by his student Arrian early in the second century). In a diatribe the teacher addresses an imaginary conversation partner, raises objections in that person's voice, and answers them, often rejecting a false conclusion with an emphatic ‘By no means’. Rudolf Bultmann's 1910 dissertation compared Paul's style with the Cynic-Stoic diatribe, and Stanley Stowers (The Diatribe and Paul's Letter to the Romans, 1981) showed that the diatribe belonged to the classroom, used to instruct students, not to attack real opponents.

Romans is full of it. Paul suddenly turns to address ‘you’ in the singular: “You, therefore, have no excuse, you who pass judgment on another.” (Romans 2:1); “Now you, if you call yourself a Jew” (2:17). He raises objections and answers them: “What then shall we say? Shall we continue in sin so that grace may increase? Certainly not!” (6:1-2). The Greek phrase behind ‘Certainly not’ is mē genoito, the diatribe's emphatic rejection, which older translations rendered ‘God forbid’. A reader who does not notice the form may take the imagined objector's words as Paul's own view.

Something similar happens in 1 Corinthians, where Paul seems to quote slogans current in Corinth in order to answer them. The original Greek had no quotation marks, and translations must decide where they belong. Most modern versions put “Everything is permissible for me” in quotation marks in 1 Corinthians 6:12 as a Corinthian saying that Paul qualifies. In 7:1, translations differ: some print ‘It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman’ as a quotation from the Corinthians' letter that Paul then answers; others, including the Berean Standard Bible (“It is good to abstain from sexual relations”), present it as Paul's own statement. The difference affects how the whole chapter on marriage is read.

Reading a New Testament letter is like hearing one side of a telephone call. The writer and the first readers shared a great deal that neither needed to say: what had happened in the church, what questions had been asked, what the writer had taught on an earlier visit. Paul refers to an earlier letter to Corinth that has not survived (1 Corinthians 5:9), to a letter the Corinthians wrote him (“Now for the matters you wrote about”, 7:1), and to reports brought by “some from Chloe’s household” (1:11). He tells the Colossians to read a letter from Laodicea that we do not have. The letters are occasional documents, written for particular occasions, and they answer questions we have to reconstruct.

Scholars call the process of reconstructing the other side mirror-reading: inferring from what the writer says what the readers were saying or doing. It is necessary and risky. John Barclay, in a 1987 article on mirror-reading a polemical letter (focused on Galatians), warned against assuming that every statement answers a specific charge or that every warning reflects a real error, and he proposed criteria: give more weight to what is stated clearly, repeated, and emphasized, and be cautious about building a picture of the opponents from a single phrase.

Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart, in How to Read the Bible for All Its Worth, put the basic rule simply: a text cannot mean what it never could have meant to its author and first readers. The first task is to hear what the letter said to them. Only then comes the second task, asking what it says now. Where our situation closely matches theirs, the application is direct; Paul's words on grace, on the resurrection, and on love need little adjustment. Where the situation is different, the reader must find the principle the text applies and ask how it applies in a new setting. Paul's instructions about meat sacrificed to idols (1 Corinthians 8 to 10) address a situation few modern Western readers face, but the principle of limiting one's own freedom for the sake of a weaker brother or sister does not depend on the market in Corinth.

Christians disagree about how to tell which instructions are bound to their culture. The holy kiss (Romans 16:16) is almost universally treated as a cultural form of a lasting principle of warm greeting; head coverings in worship (1 Corinthians 11:2-16) are treated differently by different churches; and the questions of women's ministry and of husbands and wives are sharply debated. William Webb (Slaves, Women and Homosexuals, 2001) proposed a redemptive-movement approach that follows the direction in which the New Testament moves beyond its culture; Wayne Grudem and others have criticized that approach as placing the reader's ethic above the text. These are second-order questions on which faithful churches differ, and the next section sets out the main positions on the household codes.

Several letters contain instructions to the members of a household, arranged in pairs: wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters. Scholars call them household codes, borrowing the German term Haustafeln, ‘house tables’, which Luther had used for the table of duties in his Small Catechism (1529). The main examples are Colossians 3:18 to 4:1, Ephesians 5:21 to 6:9, and 1 Peter 2:13 to 3:7, with related instructions in 1 Timothy and Titus.

The form was not invented by the apostles. Aristotle, in the first book of his Politics, discussed household management in exactly these three pairs, husband and wife, father and children, master and slave, and treated the household as the building block of the city. Hellenistic Jewish writers such as Philo and Josephus used similar lists to describe the orderly Jewish household. The New Testament codes take up this familiar pattern and change it in several ways. They address the subordinate members, wives, children, and slaves, directly, as moral persons responsible before God, which Aristotle's discussion did not do. They make the duties reciprocal: “Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord. Husbands, love your wives and do not be harsh with them.” (Colossians 3:18-19). They place every relationship under Christ: masters are told they “also have a Master in heaven” (Colossians 4:1), with whom “there is no favoritism” (Ephesians 6:9). Ephesians heads its code with a call for all believers to “Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ.” (Ephesians 5:21), and defines the husband's role by Christ's self-giving love for the church. And Philemon, the letter that sends the slave Onesimus back to his master, asks Philemon to receive him “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 16).

Scholars debate what the codes were for. David Balch (Let Wives Be Submissive, 1981) argued that in 1 Peter they served an apologetic purpose, reassuring a suspicious society that Christians were not undermining the household order. John H. Elliott (A Home for the Homeless, 1981) argued instead that they strengthened the internal life of the Christian community as a household of God distinct from its surroundings. Both concerns may be present.

Christians today read the codes in different ways, especially on marriage. Complementarians, represented by the essays in John Piper and Wayne Grudem's Recovering Biblical Manhood and Womanhood (1991), hold that the husband's loving headship and the wife's submission reflect a created order and remain the pattern for Christian marriage, while insisting that headship means sacrificial service, never domination. Egalitarians, represented by the essays in Discovering Biblical Equality (2004, edited by Ronald Pierce and Rebecca Merrill Groothuis with Gordon Fee), hold that the codes are a missional accommodation to the social structures of the time, which the gospel was already beginning to transform, and that mutual submission and the equality of Galatians 3:28, “There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus”, point to partnership in marriage. Both sides agree that the codes forbid abuse and that the husband's model is Christ, who gave himself.

The instructions to slaves raise a different and painful history. Slavery in the Roman world was not based on race, and freeing slaves was common, but it was brutal, and slaves had few protections. The New Testament regulates slavery within the church without calling for its abolition in society, while planting principles, the equal dignity of slave and master before God and the brotherhood of believers, that later Christians drew on to oppose it. In the American debates of the nineteenth century, defenders of slavery cited the household codes, and abolitionists appealed to Philemon, to Galatians 3:28, and to the condemnation of slave traders in 1 Timothy 1:10. Mark Noll (The Civil War as a Theological Crisis, 2006) traced how that conflict exposed the limits of reading isolated texts without attention to the Bible's whole witness. Nearly all Christians today agree that the codes' acceptance of slavery described their world and did not endorse the institution for all time; the debate over how far the same reasoning applies to marriage is a live one.

sections.h: Letters beyond Paul, and questions of authorship
sections.body:
The letters that follow Paul's in the New Testament are often called the General or Catholic Letters (from the Greek for ‘universal’), because most are addressed to wider audiences rather than to a single church. They vary widely in form. Hebrews has no opening greeting and calls itself “my word of exhortation” (Hebrews 13:22); most scholars read it as a written sermon with a letter's ending. James reads like a collection of wisdom teaching and exhortation, with the letter form only in its opening line. 1 Peter is a true circular letter to believers scattered across five provinces of Asia Minor. 2 Peter has the character of a testament, a farewell speech of a dying leader. Jude quotes the non-canonical book of 1 Enoch (Jude 14-15). 1 John has no opening or closing and reads like a pastoral tract; 2 and 3 John are the shortest books in the Bible, each the length of a single papyrus sheet.

The authorship of several letters is debated. Scholars generally divide Paul's thirteen letters into three groups. Seven are accepted as Paul's by nearly all scholars: Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, and Philemon. Three are disputed: 2 Thessalonians, Colossians, and Ephesians, which differ from the undisputed letters in style or emphasis. The three Pastoral Letters, 1 and 2 Timothy and Titus, are the most widely doubted, because their vocabulary, their concern with church order, and the situations they assume are hard to fit into Paul's life as Acts records it. Many critical scholars regard these letters as written after Paul's death by followers writing in his name, a practice called pseudepigraphy that was common in the ancient world. Others, among them Donald Guthrie, Luke Timothy Johnson (in his Anchor Bible commentary on 1 and 2 Timothy, 2001), and many evangelical scholars, defend Paul's authorship, pointing to the role of secretaries, to the different occasions and recipients, and to evidence that the early church rejected writings it knew to be forged; Tertullian reports that the presbyter who wrote the Acts of Paul in Paul's name was removed from office (On Baptism 17). I. Howard Marshall, in his commentary on the Pastoral Letters (1999), proposed a middle view he called allonymity: letters written by a close associate after Paul's death, using his material, without the intent to deceive. Similar debates surround 2 Peter, James, and Jude.

The author of Hebrews is unknown. Churches in the East often attributed it to Paul, which is why it was placed among his letters; Tertullian suggested Barnabas; Luther suggested Apollos; and Origen, as Eusebius reports (Church History 6.25), concluded that only God knows who wrote it. Its authority in the church has never depended on the answer.

The single best habit is to read a letter whole, at a sitting, as its first hearers did. Most of the letters can be read aloud in less than an hour, and many in a few minutes. Reading in fragments, a verse at a time, cuts the argument into pieces and invites the misreadings that 2 Peter already warned about.

Follow the argument. Paul's letters are dense with connecting words, ‘therefore’, ‘for’, ‘but’, ‘so then’, and each one tells the reader how a sentence relates to the one before. Where a ‘therefore’ appears, ask what it is there for. Notice the large movement many letters make from what God has done to what believers are to do: Romans 1 to 11 before Romans 12 to 16, Ephesians 1 to 3 before Ephesians 4 to 6. Grammarians call these the indicative (what is true) and the imperative (what to do), and the order matters: the commands grow out of grace, not the other way round.

Reconstruct the situation carefully, using the letter itself, the book of Acts where it helps, and the introductions in this Study Bible, without building more than the evidence will bear. Listen for the tone: Galatians is angry, Philippians warm, 2 Corinthians wounded, Philemon tactful. And remember that these were letters between people who loved each other, or were trying to. They end with names, Phoebe, Prisca and Aquila, Andronicus and Junia, Tertius, Erastus, Quartus, and with greetings and blessings. The theology of the letters was written for congregations of real people, and it is meant to be lived in the same way.
